claims.text: The proposed material is a NiTi-based shape memory alloy.
Controlled microstructural modifications can tune the martensitic transformation temperature of NiTi-based alloys.
Combining such modifications with in situ mechanical loading will produce a reversible and predictable temperature-dependent shift in plastic-deformation mechanisms.
The initial NiTi alloy is martensitic at lower temperatures.
The NiTi alloy transforms to austenite as temperature increases.
In situ high-resolution mechanical testing can monitor mechanical response and phase transitions under controlled temperature.
The mechanical-testing temperature range will span the martensite-to-austenite transformation.
Strain rate will be controlled during testing.
Deformation involves martensitic twin-boundary reorientation and variant redistribution.
The temperature-dependent change between martensite and austenite alters dislocation mobility.
The temperature-dependent change between martensite and austenite alters twinning activity.
Changes in dislocation mobility and twinning activity produce distinct plastic-deformation behaviors at different temperatures.
Below the transformation point, deformation is dominated by martensitic plasticity and may be more localized.
Above the transformation point, austenitic behavior produces a more uniform and ductile plastic response.
The change in deformation mechanism is reversible during temperature cycling.
Conventional fixed-temperature testing of NiTi shows standard shape-memory behavior without clearly delineating changes in plastic-deformation mechanisms during temperature transitions.
Compositional heterogeneity and processing-induced microstructural inconsistencies may limit the proposed effect.
The magnitude and reversibility of the mechanism shift may depend strongly on sample preparation and testing conditions.
